Every point here states its own risk and names when NOT to use it: negative inversion, conditional inversion and cleft/fronting overuse are net-negative in a band-6 answer and the content says so out loud.

points.title: Giving the other side one point on purpose so your own point lands harder

point_json.grammar_name: Concession structures: while it is true that, admittedly, granted

teach.can_do: I can hand the other side one point on purpose and then take the argument back.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the shape of a band-7 body paragraph. The risk is small: concede once and answer it. Concede twice with no answer and you have changed sides.
teach.meaning: A concession frame hands the other side one point, out loud, before you answer it. It is not politeness and it is not weakness. It tells your reader you have read the argument you are about to beat, which is why the answer that follows lands harder than a flat denial would. The frame has two halves and the second half is compulsory: the point you give away, then the reason it does not decide the question.

form.pattern: While it is true that + CLAUSE , + your answer    |    Admittedly / Granted , + CLAUSE . However , + your answer
notes: the point you give away comes first and the answer comes second, never the other way round
while it is true that needs a whole clause after it; granted and admittedly stand alone with a comma
one frame in a paragraph reads as an argument, two in the same paragraph read as agreement
the relation is marked once: no but after although, no however after while
form.negative: Nobody would deny that + CLAUSE , but + your answer
form.question: Ask yourself: what is the strongest thing they have, and can I survive saying it out loud?

right.text: almost none of that work lasts past September

spec.caption: The first box is a gift. It is only worth giving if the second box is heavier.

worked_example.sentence: While it is true that the resorts have brought year-round work to the coast, most of those posts are filled from outside the district.

notice_set.sentence: Granted, the ferry is cheaper. It also takes four hours longer than the bridge.

notice_set.question: Does the speaker think the museum has solved the town's problem?

notice_set.question: Has the speaker finished making their point?
notice_set.why: A point handed to the other side on its own is just a point for the other side. The answer has not arrived yet.

notice_set.question: How does the speaker feel about the project now?
notice_set.why: The hard winter is given away and the second winter is kept, and what a speaker keeps is what they mean.

discovery.prompt: On the left and on the right the two facts are identical. What has changed about the situation the writer is standing in?

While the resorts brought work, most of the posts went to outsiders.
Granted, the ferry is cheaper. It also takes four hours longer.

On the left, the writer is being polite about the other side.
On the left, the sentence has an extra word or two in front of the first fact.

teach.rule_line: Hand over the strongest thing they have, then take the argument back in the same breath.
teach.false_rule: That a concession makes you sound balanced. It only does that if the answer arrives. Left alone, it is the other side's sentence with your name on it.

contrast.question: Am I answering an argument, or just putting two facts side by side?

fork.answer: Two facts, side by side, and nobody is arguing about either of them
fork.selects: a plain contrast marker: whereas, while, on the other hand

fork.answer: One short fact that goes against me, and I want it out of the way inside the same sentence
fork.selects: despite or although in front of the fact

fork.answer: A whole argument on the other side that I intend to answer
fork.selects: a concession frame: while it is true that ... , ...

a.text: While it is true that the industry creates jobs, most of those jobs last one season.
a.means: Somebody has offered the jobs as an argument. The writer has taken it seriously, said it back, and is now answering it.

b.text: While the industry creates jobs, most of those jobs last one season.
b.means: Two facts placed side by side. The reader is told the jobs exist and that they are seasonal, and is left to weigh them.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You chose the plain marker. That tells your reader nobody has argued the first half, so your paragraph reads as a description of a situation rather than as an answer to somebody. The argument you were having disappears.

edge_case.text: In Speaking Part 3 the same move is made with I mean, yes, but and fair enough, though. The frame is different and the move is identical. Know that, then leave those versions in speech.

contrast.stronger_test: Cover the second half of your sentence. If what is left is something you would be unhappy for a reader to think you believe, you have conceded. If it is just a fact, you have only contrasted.

worked_pairs.a: While it is true that visitors spend heavily in the old town, the money leaves on the six o'clock coach.
worked_pairs.b: While visitors spend heavily in the old town, the shops in the outer streets see none of it.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: the shops in the outer streets
worked_pairs.gloss: The first answers somebody who has offered the spending as proof. The second reports two facts about two different parts of a town.

worked_pairs.a: Granted, the festival fills the hotels, but the town pays for the clean-up all year.
worked_pairs.b: The festival fills the hotels, whereas the campsite stands empty until August.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first gives away a point in an argument. The second compares two places and takes nobody's side.

worked_pairs.a: Nobody would deny that the port created work; the question is who it created work for.
worked_pairs.b: The port created work, and the fishing fleet lost half its crew in the same decade.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first hands over the jobs so that the next clause can reopen the argument. The second simply reports two things that happened together.

errors.wrong: Although the resorts brought work to the coast, but the posts went to outsiders.
errors.right: Although the resorts brought work to the coast, the posts went to outsiders.
errors.why_it_happens: Many languages mark a contrast at both ends of the sentence, so a bare second half feels unfinished and the hand reaches for but before the writer has noticed the marker already sitting at the front.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: but.
errors.l1_note: Very frequent where the first language marks contrast twice.

errors.wrong: Despite it is true that the fee is high, the road it pays for carries every lorry in the district.
errors.right: Although it is true that the fee is high, the road it pays for carries every lorry in the district.
errors.why_it_happens: Despite and although land on the same single word in many languages, and the concession frame that follows is a whole clause, which despite has no way of holding.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: Despite becomes Although.

errors.wrong: Admittedly, the cost was high. Admittedly, the delays were long.
errors.right: Admittedly, the cost was high. The delays were long too.
errors.why_it_happens: It has been stored as a way to start a sentence rather than as a move you make exactly once, so it fires everywhere and the writer finishes by arguing for the other side.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: the second Admittedly.

errors.wrong: Yeah, ok, the money does come in, but still.
errors.right: It is true that the money comes in, but very little of it stays.
errors.why_it_happens: The spoken version of this move is a shrug and a filler, and under time pressure the spoken version is the one that arrives first because it is the one the writer actually says.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one frame: Yeah, ok becomes It is true that.

points.title: Telling your reader how far you are willing to back what you just said

point_json.grammar_name: Stance and evaluation adverbials: arguably, crucially, to a large extent, on balance

teach.can_do: I can say how far I am backing a claim without writing I think.
teach.why_it_matters: One word, well placed, does the work of a whole hedging clause. The risk is real: four of them in a paragraph and nothing you write carries any weight.
teach.meaning: These words do not add facts. They tell your reader what to do with the fact you have just given them: how likely you think it is, how much of it holds, or how much weight it should carry in the argument. That is why one of them can change a paragraph without changing a single claim in it, and why the wrong one quietly reports a position you do not hold.

form.pattern: ADVERBIAL , + CLAUSE    |    SUBJECT + ADVERBIAL + VERB    |    CLAUSE , + ADVERBIAL
notes: at the front it colours the whole sentence; in the middle it colours the verb only
a comma after it at the front, and a comma on each side in the middle
one to a sentence, and rarely more than two in a paragraph
arguably, crucially and on balance belong on the page; to be fair and to be honest belong in speech
form.negative: The word sits inside what you are denying: write it is arguably not the strongest case, not it is not arguably the strongest case.
form.question: Ask yourself: am I rating how likely this is, how much of it holds, or how much it matters?

spec.label: how far am I backing this?

steps.gloss: I will not be argued out of this
the evidence is already in front of you
I hold this, and I expect somebody to argue
most of it holds; some of it does not
I have weighed both sides and this side wins

worked_example.sentence: Longer sentences arguably deter a first offence, but they do very little about a second.
worked_example.why_this_form: The writer holds the position and knows the figures get read both ways, so the word admits the argument without giving the claim away.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Longer sentences may deter a first offence would say the writer does not know whether the effect exists at all, which is a much weaker thing to have written.

notice_set.sentence: On balance, the evening patrols have been worth what they cost.
notice_set.question: Has the speaker found anything wrong with the patrols?
notice_set.why: You only balance something when there is weight on both sides, so something has been put on the other one.

notice_set.sentence: The patrols helped, but crucially, they were paired with a place for teenagers to go.
notice_set.question: Which part does the speaker think mattered most?
notice_set.why: The word marks the part that carries the argument, and it is standing right next to the pairing.

notice_set.sentence: To a large extent, the fall in thefts follows the new street lighting.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker think the lighting explains the whole fall?
notice_set.why: Most of it, not all of it. The words leave room for something else to explain the rest.

notice_set.sentence: Arguably, the scheme should never have been funded at all.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker expect everyone to agree with them?
notice_set.why: The word invites the argument it is expecting, which is why it does not sound the same as saying it flat.

notice_set.sentence: Undoubtedly, the scheme has cost more than the courts it replaced.
notice_set.question: How sure is the speaker?
notice_set.why: Nothing has been left open, so if the figure turns out to be wrong the sentence has nowhere left to go.

teach.rule_line: Say how far you are backing it, then let the sentence carry the claim.
teach.false_rule: That these words make writing sound academic. They mark a position. Put one on a claim nobody disputes and your reader hears somebody defending an empty room.

contrast.question: Am I rating how likely it is, or how much of it holds?

fork.answer: How likely it is that this happens at all
fork.selects: a modal hedge: may, tends to, is likely to

fork.answer: How much of it holds — most of it, or every bit of it
fork.selects: a degree adverbial: to a large extent, broadly, on balance

fork.answer: How much weight it should carry in my argument
fork.selects: an evaluative adverbial: crucially, arguably, more importantly

a.means: The writer does not know whether it happens. They are reporting a possibility somebody else can take or leave.

b.means: The writer thinks it does happen and is telling you, in advance, that they expect to be argued with about it.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote may. That tells the examiner you are not sure the effect exists, so everything you build on it stands on a maybe. You did know; you were expecting an argument. Those are different things, and only one of them is a position.

edge_case.text: In speech the same job is done by to be fair, I'd say and probably, and those are right where they are. Moving them onto a Task 2 page costs you the mark you were reaching for.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask what you would do if somebody showed you a study going the other way. If you would drop the claim, you needed the hedge. If you would argue, you needed arguably.

worked_pairs.a: On balance, the evening patrols were worth what they cost.

worked_pairs.a: To a large extent, the fall in thefts follows the new lighting.
worked_pairs.b: The fall in thefts follows the new lighting.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first leaves room for another cause and survives one awkward figure. The second is destroyed by it.

errors.wrong: Prison makes offenders worse.
errors.right: Prison arguably makes offenders worse.
errors.why_it_happens: A strong flat sentence feels like a strong argument, so the claim goes in bare. One counter-example then takes the whole paragraph down with it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: arguably.

errors.wrong: It is not arguably the strongest case for the scheme.
errors.right: It is arguably not the strongest case for the scheme.
errors.why_it_happens: The negative goes in front of everything out of habit, and the marker ends up inside the part being denied, so the sentence denies the writer's own hedge instead of the claim.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: arguably goes in front of not.

errors.wrong: Arguably, the patrols worked. Arguably, the lighting helped.
errors.right: Arguably, the patrols worked. The lighting helped too.
errors.why_it_happens: The word has been drilled as a sentence opener rather than as a mark you place on a single disputed claim, so it lands on everything and marks nothing.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: the second arguably.

errors.wrong: To be honest, the scheme was a waste of money.
errors.right: On balance, the scheme did not justify what it cost.
errors.why_it_happens: The spoken marker arrives first under time pressure because it is the one the writer actually says, and on the page it reads as an aside to a friend rather than a judgement.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one frame: To be honest becomes On balance.

points.title: Choosing the grammar that fits the room you are in

point_json.grammar_name: Register: spoken grammar and written grammar

teach.can_do: I can tell which grammar belongs in the speaking room and which belongs on the page.
teach.why_it_matters: Learners lose marks twice over here: spoken grammar in Task 2, and essay grammar in Part 1, where a friendly question gets answered by a press release.
teach.meaning: Speaking and writing are not the same language at different volumes. Real-time speech joins short clauses with and and so, contracts whatever it can, reaches for get where writing reaches for be, and leaves out anything both people can already see. Writing has a reader who cannot ask you to say it again, so it packs more into each sentence, spells the small words out and marks the joins. Neither is better English. Each is wrong in the other room.

form.pattern: spoken: contractions + get-passive + two-word verbs + and / so    |    written: full forms + be-passive + single-word verbs + subordinators
notes: the ferry got cancelled belongs in an ear; the ferry was cancelled belongs on a page
don't, can't and it's are right in Part 1 and cost you something in Task 2
put off, sort out and go up out loud; postpone, resolve and rise on the page
a letter to a friend in GT Task 1 is spoken grammar written down, on purpose
form.negative: isn't and hasn't out loud; is not and has not on the page. Same meaning, different room.
form.question: Ask yourself which room the sentence is walking into before you build it.

points.title: Putting the one part that matters where nobody can read past it

point_json.grammar_name: Emphasis in production: clefts and fronting

teach.can_do: I can lift one part of a sentence into the light, and I know when not to.
teach.why_it_matters: Used once, at the point of disagreement, it marks your real claim. Used three times it cancels itself out. If nothing is in dispute, write the plain sentence.
teach.meaning: You already know how to build these shapes. This point is about deciding, inside a real paragraph, which part of a sentence needs lifting out, which shape to lift it with, and — far more often — deciding not to. English has three ways of putting one part under a light: it is X that, what the clause is is X, and simply moving X to the front. They cost different amounts of the reader's patience and they belong in different rooms.

form.pattern: It + is / was + X + that / who + REST    |    What + CLAUSE + is / was + X    |    X , + SUBJECT + VERB
notes: the it shape puts the part in the light first; the what shape holds it back until the end
moving the part to the front is the cheap version and the rest of the sentence stays as it was
the fronted version is at home out loud; the two longer shapes are at home on a page
no extra pronoun after a fronted part, and no comma before that in the it shape

points.title: Opening on a negative word and swapping the next two round

point_json.grammar_name: Inversion after negative and restrictive adverbials

teach.can_do: I can turn a sentence round after an opening negative, and I know when not to.
teach.why_it_matters: Four things must be right at once and the reward is one sentence. If your ordinary sentences are not yet clean, leave this one alone and spend the nerve elsewhere.
teach.meaning: When a sentence opens on a word meaning never, rarely, only or not, English turns the next two words round: the small helping word jumps in front of the subject, exactly as it does in a question. The sentence is not a question and nothing about what it claims has changed. What has changed is where your reader's attention starts — on the never rather than on the person — which is why it reads as a claim being pressed rather than reported.

form.pattern: NEGATIVE OPENER + AUXILIARY + SUBJECT + MAIN VERB
notes: if there is no auxiliary in the sentence already, do, does or did comes in to be moved, exactly as in a question
rarely does a lender admit it; never had the charge been waived; only after the inquiry did the figures change
the turn happens once, in the clause the negative word opens, and nowhere else
not only X but also Y turns the first half only: not only did costs rise, but the service also got slower
form.negative: The negative is already in the opening word, so the verb itself stays positive: never has the fee been waived.
form.question: Ask yourself: is my first word never, rarely, seldom, only, not once, or under no circumstances?

left.text: the fund has rarely paid out in full

right.text: rarely has the fund paid out in full

spec.caption: The words are the same and the claim is the same. Only the first thing your reader meets has changed.

worked_example.sentence: Rarely has a scheme of this size come in under its own forecast.
worked_example.why_this_form: The paragraph is arguing that overspending is normal, so the sentence has to open on how unusual it is rather than on the scheme.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: A scheme of this size has rarely come in under its own forecast makes the identical claim and starts the reader on the scheme, which is not where the argument is.

notice_set.sentence: Not once has the fund paid out in full.

teach.rule_line: After an opening negative, put the helping word in front of the subject.
teach.false_rule: That this makes a sentence sound advanced. It makes a claim sound pressed, and in an answer where nothing is being pressed it reads as somebody shouting in a library.

errors.wrong: Under no circumstances the fee can be waived.

errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: can goes in front of the fee.

errors.wrong: Rarely do the fund pay out in full.
errors.right: Rarely does the fund pay out in full.
errors.why_it_happens: The helping word is chosen before the writer has looked past the opener to see what the subject actually is, and the commoner form arrives first.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: do becomes does.

errors.wrong: Not only must the firm to pay a fine, but it also loses the contract.
errors.right: Not only must the firm pay a fine, but it also loses the contract.
errors.why_it_happens: Once the order has been turned round, the writer loses track of which word the main verb is hanging from, and the default to arrives in front of it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: to.

errors.wrong: Never have I seen a garden as fine as that one.
errors.right: I've never seen a garden that nice.
errors.why_it_happens: The shape has been drilled for essays and arrives in Part 1, where an ordinary friendly question has been asked and the answer comes back sounding like a speech.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one frame: Never have I.

rarely does the ferry run in weather like this.

meanings: The timing is what the writer is pressing, and the reader meets it before anything else.
The same fact, reported evenly, with the figures as the thing the sentence is about.

feedback.why_key: Both sentences are true and both are correct. One presses the timing at the reader; the other simply reports it in passing.
feedback.feed_forward: Front the opener only when the timing is the argument.

feedback.why_key: Opening on the rarity puts the argument in the reader's first three words instead of burying it in the middle of the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Open on the negative word, then jump the subject.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on funding for space research. Find the single sentence where you press hardest and turn that one round after a negative opener. Check the helping word matches the subject, then leave every other sentence exactly as it is. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: One of these in an essay is a raised voice at the right moment. Three of them is a candidate who shouts through the whole answer.
feedback.feed_forward: Use it once, where you press hardest, then stop.

points.title: Dropping if and starting the sentence with had

point_json.grammar_name: Conditional inversion: had, were and should at the front

teach.can_do: I can write an unreal past sentence without using if, and I know what it buys me.
teach.why_it_matters: It buys one thing: a formal sentence with no if in it. If the third conditional is not yet automatic, spend the nerve on something that pays more.
teach.meaning: This is the same unreal sentence you already build with if, with the if taken out and the had moved to the front. Nothing about the meaning moves: the thing did not happen, and the sentence says what would have followed if it had. What changes is only how it sounds — heavier, more written, a little more formal than the same idea with if in it. That is the whole return, which is why the rest of the sentence has to be perfect.

form.pattern: Had + SUBJECT + past participle , + would have + past participle    |    Were + SUBJECT + to + VERB , ...    |    Should + SUBJECT + VERB , ...
notes: the if disappears; it never sits in front of had
had the licence been renewed, the office would not have lost a week of work
the negative is not shortened at the front: had it not been for the backup, never hadn't it been for the backup
should at the front is the polite one about a thing that might still happen: should you need help, call the desk
form.negative: Had the team not tested it — the not goes after the subject, and had never shortens at the front of the sentence.
form.question: Ask yourself whether you could write the same sentence with if. If you could not, this shape will not rescue it.

marks.label: the outage would have lasted an hour

worked_example.sentence: Had the update been tested on one machine first, the outage would have lasted an hour rather than a week.
worked_example.why_this_form: The paragraph already has two sentences beginning with if, and this version makes the same unreal claim without adding a third.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: If the update had been tested on one machine first carries an identical claim in a slightly lighter voice, and loses the writer nothing at all.

notice_set.sentence: Had the backup run that night, the records would still exist.
notice_set.question: Do the records still exist?
notice_set.why: The whole sentence is about a night that went differently, so the records went with it.

notice_set.sentence: Had the update been tested, the outage would have lasted an hour.
notice_set.question: How long did the outage actually last?
notice_set.why: The one-hour outage is the version that never occurred, so the real one must have run longer than that.

notice_set.sentence: Should you need a replacement, the desk will order one.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker know that you need a replacement?
notice_set.why: This one is about something that might still happen, not about something that did not.

notice_set.sentence: Were the system rebuilt today, it would still run the same software.
notice_set.question: Is anyone rebuilding the system?
notice_set.why: The rebuild is imagined in order to make a point about the software, which means nobody is actually doing it.

notice_set.sentence: Had it not been for the paper records, the whole month would have been lost.
notice_set.question: Was the month lost?
notice_set.why: The paper records are the reason it was not, and saying so is the only reason this sentence exists.

teach.rule_line: Take out if, move had to the front, and change nothing else in the sentence.
teach.false_rule: That this is a more advanced conditional. It is the same conditional wearing a coat, and the version with if scores exactly the same when it is clean.

errors.wrong: Have the alarm been fitted, the loss would have been far smaller.
errors.right: Had the alarm been fitted, the loss would have been far smaller.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows the shape opens on a form of have and reaches for the one they use most often, and the sentence loses the very word that made it unreal.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: Have becomes Had.

errors.wrong: If had the council acted sooner, the cost would have been lower.
errors.right: Had the council acted sooner, the cost would have been lower.
errors.why_it_happens: The shape is learned as an extra thing you add to a conditional rather than as a replacement for the if, so both markers end up in the same sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: If.

errors.wrong: Had the team would have tested it, the outage would have been shorter.
errors.right: Had the team tested it, the outage would have been shorter.
errors.why_it_happens: Would have belongs in the other half of the sentence, and once the order is turned round the writer loses track of which half they are standing in.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two words: would have, from the first half.

errors.wrong: Had the licence been renewed, the office would lose no time at all.
errors.right: Had the licence been renewed, the office would have lost no time at all.
errors.why_it_happens: The first half is safely in the unreal past and the second half slides into the present unreal, because would arrives before the writer has settled which time they are in.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: have, after would.

pays_in.note: It breaks up a paragraph in which every sentence has started with if.
pays_in.model: Had the scheme been funded for a second year, the results would have been worth reading.

pays_in.note: Should you need is the standard polite offer at the end of a formal letter.
pays_in.model: Should you require any further information, please contact me at the address above.

pays_in.note: A fronted had signals an unreal past, and a reader who misses it takes away the opposite fact.
pays_in.model: Had the second alarm been fitted, the fire would have been caught in minutes.

used_in.quote: The second half of this prompt asks what would have kept students in science, which is an unreal past claim in every paragraph.

payload.question: Do the records still exist?

feedback.why_key: The sentence is built around a night that went the other way, and everything in it follows from that night not having happened.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the first half as something that did not happen.

payload.sentence: Should you need a replacement, the desk will order one.
payload.question: Does the writer know that you need a replacement?

feedback.why_key: This opener is about something that might still happen, so nothing has been decided and nothing has been ruled out yet.
feedback.feed_forward: Separate the might-happen opener from the did-not-happen one.

payload.sentence: If had the office renewed the licence, no time would have been lost.
reasons: the sentence marks the condition twice
the second half is in the wrong time
the first half needs a comma
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The moved had is doing the job that if used to do. Keeping both leaves the reader with two openers and one condition.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose one marker: either if or the moved had.

payload.context: From a report on an outage that lasted a week. Nobody tested the update.
payload.stem: ___ the update been tested on one machine first, the outage would have lasted an hour.

expected: had

feedback.why_key: The past form is the word that makes the sentence unreal. Any other form of it puts the testing back into the real world.

payload.given: If the warning had been passed on, the crew would have turned back.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it without the word if.

expected: the warning been passed on, the crew would have turned back
the warning been passed on the crew would have turned back

feedback.why_key: Only two things moved: if left and had came forward. Every other word in the sentence stayed exactly where it was.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap if for a fronted had and touch nothing else.

payload.given: Had the second year been funded, the results would have been worth reading.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it with if, keeping the meaning identical.

expected: the second year had been funded, the results would have been worth reading

payload.context: Build the closing line of a formal letter.

expected: should you need any further information please contact the desk

feedback.why_key: The opener takes the subject straight after it and a plain verb after that. Nothing is added and no if appears anywhere.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the subject directly after the opening word.

payload.audio_text: Had we tested it first, we'd have caught it in an hour.

expected: had we tested it first, we'd have caught it in an hour
had we tested it first, we would have caught it in an hour

points.title: Spending your last three minutes on the mistakes that cost most

point_json.grammar_name: Self-editing: the four end checks, in priority order

teach.can_do: I can spend my last three minutes on the four mistakes that cost most, in order.
teach.why_it_matters: Accuracy at the end of a timed task is a procedure, not a feeling. Reading it through again finds almost nothing; running four named checks finds most of it.
teach.meaning: At the end of a timed task you have no attention left for everything at once, and reading the whole answer through again is the least useful thing you can do with three minutes, because your eye quietly repairs whatever you meant to write. What works instead is four separate passes, each hunting one thing only, run in the order in which the mistakes cost you most. Four narrow sweeps beat one wide one, every time, and they can be practised.

form.pattern: 1 where each sentence ends  →  2 each verb against its own subject  →  3 one time per paragraph  →  4 the small words in front of singular nouns
notes: check one: every sentence ends on a full stop, and no comma is doing a full stop's job
check two: put a finger on each verb and trace it back to its own subject, ignoring everything sitting in between
check three: read only the verbs of one paragraph, in order, and see whether they stay in one time
check four: for every singular countable noun, ask what is standing in front of it
form.negative: Do not read for meaning during these three minutes. Reading for meaning is exactly what hides the mistakes from you.
form.question: Ask yourself which of the four you are running right now. If the answer is all of them, you are running none of them.

spec.label: what does it cost if you leave it?

steps.gloss: your reader loses the sentence itself, so fix this one first

steps.text: each verb against its own subject
steps.gloss: visible in almost every line and quick to repair
your reader has to re-date every claim you make
costs least and takes longest, so it goes last

worked_example.sentence: The number of families sharing a home has risen. This is partly because rents in the city have doubled.
worked_example.why_this_form: Two of the four checks caught two separate things here: a comma holding two whole pieces of news together, and two verbs that had each copied the nearest noun.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Left alone, a reader meets one long run of words with no clear claim in it and decides the writer cannot see their own sentences, which is a much larger judgement than one comma deserves.

notice_set.sentence: The number of families sharing a home have risen sharply.
notice_set.question: How many things is the writer counting here?
notice_set.why: What rose is a count, and a count stays single no matter how many families it is counting.

notice_set.sentence: Rents in the city has doubled since the mill closed.
notice_set.question: What doubled?
notice_set.why: The rents are what doubled. The city is only where they are, and it has ended up standing next to the wrong word.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme was popular, it closed after two years.
notice_set.question: How many separate pieces of news is the writer giving you?
notice_set.why: Two whole pieces of news are leaning on one comma, and a comma cannot take that weight.

notice_set.sentence: Grandparents used to live nearby. Now families move away for work and the children only saw them twice a year.
notice_set.question: Is the writer talking about the past or about now?
notice_set.why: The writer moves from an old arrangement to the present one, and one word at the end is still standing in the wrong half.

notice_set.sentence: She works as nurse in a hospital near the coast.
notice_set.question: Is anything missing from what you can picture here?
notice_set.why: One job, one person: with nothing standing in front of it, an English reader pictures the idea instead of anybody at all.

discovery.prompt: Here are three drafts, each in its last minute. What did the writer on the right do that the writer on the left did not?
pairs: The market was busy, it moved to the retail park.
The market was busy, but it moved to the retail park.
The list of names taken at the door were long.
The list of names taken at the door was long.
He trained as electrician before the yard shut.
He trained as an electrician before the yard shut.

candidate_rules.text: On the right, the writer hunted one named thing at a time instead of reading it all through.
On the right, the writer had more time left at the end.
On the right, the sentences are longer, so more care went into them.

teach.rule_line: Four narrow passes, in cost order, beat one read-through every single time.
teach.false_rule: That reading your answer through again is checking it. Your eye repairs what you meant to write, so a general read-through finds only the mistakes you were never going to make.

errors.wrong: The scheme was popular, it closed after two years.
errors.right: The scheme was popular, but it closed after two years.
errors.why_it_happens: The two halves feel like one thought, so a comma feels like enough, and under time pressure nobody stops to ask whether each half could stand up on its own.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: but, after the comma.
errors.l1_note: Standard punctuation in several European languages, so it survives long after the grammar is secure.

errors.wrong: The number of families sharing a home have risen sharply.
errors.right: The number of families sharing a home has risen sharply.
errors.why_it_happens: Families is the last noun before the verb and it is plural, so the ending copies that rather than tracing back to the number, which is the thing that actually rose.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: have becomes has.

errors.wrong: Grandparents used to live nearby. Now families move away for work and the children only saw them twice a year.
errors.right: Grandparents used to live nearby. Now families move away for work and the children only see them twice a year.
errors.why_it_happens: Each verb gets chosen on its own and nothing ever reads the paragraph as one unit, so this arrives late in a timed answer, when no attention is left to spend.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: saw becomes see.

errors.wrong: She works as nurse in a hospital near the coast.
errors.right: She works as a nurse in a hospital near the coast.
errors.why_it_happens: Many languages leave nothing in front of a job title, and the missing word changes no meaning at all, so nothing in the writer's own ear objects to it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: a, before nurse.
errors.l1_note: Persistent for speakers of languages with no articles, long after the rule is known.

pays_in.note: The last three minutes are worth more than any structure you could add instead.
pays_in.model: The number of households sharing a home has risen, and rents have doubled since the mill closed.

pays_in.note: Task 1 is dense with numbers and single nouns, which is where two of the four checks pay.
pays_in.model: The proportion of adults living alone rose steadily, whereas the figure for shared housing fell.

pays_in.note: Finding where a writer's sentence really ends is half of reading a long paragraph accurately.
pays_in.model: The trial was popular; it ended after two years for reasons nobody has explained.

used_in.quote: A two-part answer runs long, and the drift between past and present arrives in the last paragraph of it every time.
Every sentence here has a long subject with a plural noun in the middle of it, which is check two's whole hunting ground.

payload.sentence: The number of households on the waiting list has grown in every one of the last five years.
payload.question: What is the writer counting?

feedback.why_key: What went up is a count, and a count stays single however many families it happens to cover.
feedback.feed_forward: Find what the sentence is really counting before you read on.

payload.sentence: The playground was well used, it was sold for housing.
payload.question: How many separate pieces of news are you being given?

feedback.why_key: Two whole pieces of news are leaning on a single comma, which was never built to hold either of them up.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the pieces of news before you count the punctuation.

items.decision_cue: afternoon, it shut in the spring

payload.context: From the last paragraph of a timed answer, written with four minutes left.
payload.sentence: The library was busy every afternoon, it shut in the spring.
reasons: two whole pieces of news are being joined by a comma
the second half has no main verb
the two halves are in different times
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Each half could stand up on its own, which is exactly the test. Two that can stand alone need something stronger than a comma between them.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether each half could stand alone before accepting a comma.

payload.context: Check two, run over one sentence of a draft.
payload.stem: The number of children living with a grandparent ___ (rise) sharply over the last decade.

expected: has risen

feedback.why_key: Grandparent is the nearest noun and the number is the real one. Trace it back past everything in between and the ending chooses itself.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace the verb back to its own subject, past whatever sits between.

payload.context: Check four, run over one line of a Task 1 answer.
payload.stem: Her father trained as ___ electrician at the yard before it closed.

expected: an

feedback.why_key: One job and one person, so your reader needs something standing in front of that noun before they can picture anybody.
feedback.feed_forward: Check what is standing in front of each singular noun.

payload.given: The market was busy, it moved to the retail park.
payload.instruction: Repair it with the smallest edit you can make.

expected: , but it moved to the retail park
but it moved to the retail park
. It moved to the retail park
; it moved to the retail park

feedback.why_key: One word, one full stop or one semicolon. All three repairs cost the same and all three tell the reader where the first piece of news ended.
feedback.feed_forward: Repair a run-on with one mark or one word, not a rewrite.

payload.audio_text: The number of pupils walking to school has fallen again.

expected: the number of pupils walking to school has fallen again
the number of pupils walking to school has fallen again.

feedback.why_key: Has is unstressed and arrives straight after a plural noun, so a listener writing at speed puts the ending that the last word suggested.
feedback.feed_forward: Hold the subject in your head until the verb arrives.

payload.context: Build a sentence whose ending matches the proportion rather than the adults.

expected: the proportion of adults living alone has risen steadily

feedback.why_key: Four words sit between the proportion and the ending that belongs to it, and every one of them is a chance to lose track.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a long subject back to its first word before choosing.

items.decision_cue: wages in the district has fallen

payload.sentence: One reason is that wages in the district has fallen since the yard shut.
payload.error_span: wages in the district has fallen

expected: wages in the district have fallen

feedback.why_key: The district is only where the wages are paid. What fell is the wages, and the ending has copied whichever word stood nearest to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ignore whatever sits between the subject and its verb.

items.decision_cue: affordable, most of them were sold

payload.sentence: The first flats were affordable, most of them were sold to landlords within a year.

expected: affordable, but most of them
affordable. Most of them
affordable; most of them

feedback.why_key: Each half could stand on its own, so the mark between them cannot do the job, and your reader loses track of where the first claim finished.
feedback.feed_forward: Split or join with one mark, then move to the next check.

items.decision_cue: the children only visited twice a year

payload.context: Check three, run over the closing paragraph of a timed answer.
payload.sentence: Grandparents used to be a bus ride away. Now most people settle where the work is and the children only visited twice a year.
reasons: one word at the end is still standing in the earlier half
two pieces of news are joined by a comma
something is missing in front of one of the nouns
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The paragraph moves to now in its second sentence and one word never made the move, so the reader has to re-date the whole claim.
feedback.feed_forward: Read only the verbs of a paragraph, in order, and nothing else.

payload.prompt_text: Write three sentences about why fewer families now live near their grandparents. Then run check one and check two over what you wrote, in that order, and correct anything they catch before you submit.

feedback.why_key: Running the checks on your own fresh sentences is the only version of this that transfers. Somebody else's mistakes are always easier to see.
feedback.feed_forward: Run one check at a time, in order, over your own writing.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on changing careers. Run all four checks over the last body paragraph, in cost order, three minutes on the clock: where each sentence ends, each verb against its own subject, one time per paragraph, then the small words. Report what each pass caught.

feedback.why_key: The last paragraph is where the mistakes gather, because it is written with the least attention left and read with none at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Start the clock, run the four passes in order, and stop.
